An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This measure surpasses the experimental sensitivity predicted by the Standard Model and places stringent requirements on theories that introduce new particles at an energy scale higher than 100 TeV. Moreover, this measure determines the $B^0_s$ meson's instability rate to be less than 1.5 × 10^-8 at a confidence level of 95%. As a secondary discovery, LHCb found the branching fraction of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ to be (4.6 ± 0.7 ± 0.3 ± 0.5) × 10^-7. This analysis employed data from around 1.0 fb^-1 of LHCb Proton-Proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper's main section explores the stochastic aspect, with the Monte-Carlo approach yielding an estimate of the optimal control problem's solution; it also investigates the statistical properties of this estimated solution. The second part of the paper considers a related problem without stochastic noise, also involving the discretization of a diffusion equation with a prescribed boundary condition; it includes an analysis of the variance reduction technique known as the quasi-optimal finite element method. The paper's final section discusses potential future applications of these numerical methods to control problems involving stochastic processes in complex geometries. It includes an estimate of the computational time required for the Monte-Carlo and quasi-optimal finite element methods and discusses how these methods can be adapted for use with spatially dependent noise inputs. It concludes by outlining a strategy for optimizing the parameters of these numerical methods and presents some preliminary results obtained with a simpler version of the quasi-optimal finite element method. The paper also includes an appendix with additional details regarding the construction of an approximation of the stochastic algebraic operator and the properties of the quasi-optimal finite element method. It has been demonstrated that both the Monte-Carlo and quasi-optimal finite element methods yield an estimate of the optimal control problem's solution with an expected computational time of O(N) for N degrees of freedom. It also shows that the variance reduction technique can result in a significant improvement in the variance of the estimated solution, leading to a more efficient computation when combining it with the quasi-optimal finite element method. It has been acknowledged that both methods have the potential to be highly beneficial for controlling stochastic processes in complex geometries. It has been noted that the quasi-optimal finite element method can lead to substantial improvements in both the accuracy and the efficiency of the computation, while the Monte-Carlo method provides a means to achieve this through variance reduction techniques. It has been concluded that further research is needed to fully evaluate the performance of these numerical methods in the context of control problems involving stochastic processes in complex geometries. It has been also concluded that both the quasi-optimal finite element method and the Monte-Carlo method are viable options for solving the control problem with stochastic noise, while the quasi-optimal finite element method is a top candidate to solve this type of problem.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, taking into account the detectors' exposure time and the cosmic rays' arrival directions. We discovered that the anisotropy strength grows with increasing energy above 4 EeV, with an average coefficient of 2.37±0.24 (statistically significant at a 4.5σ confidence level) for the most energetic group. We also discovered that the anisotropy direction shifts from a right ascension-based modulation in the middle energy group to one based on declination in the most energetic group, with an angle of approximately 78°±9°. These findings suggest that the nature of these cosmic rays varies with energy and is connected to sources located at different positions on the sky. We cannot rule out a connection between these cosmic rays and exotic sources that are dispersed uniformly across the sky, as their spatial pattern's size is greater than 10° and comparable to the density of such sources as indicated by optical observations of active galactic nuclei targets, although we do not have sufficient statistical evidence for this hypothesis. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the anisotropy strength and the cosmic rays' energy, which could be linked to the nature of these particles or the effects of gravitational fields along the shortest paths between the sources and the detectors. We are currently working to confirm these findings with a more detailed analysis that takes into account the local matter distribution near the sources, the gravitational influence on the cosmic rays' paths, and the detectors' exposure time and sensitivity. This study's results have significant implications for our understanding of extreme energy sources and the gravitational influence on cosmic rays as they travel across the vast cosmic distance. Furthermore, we believe that our findings will be confirmed by upcoming experiments using cosmic clocks and advanced detectors at the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope. Moreover, our discovery of anisotropy in the most energetic group of cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory has implications for our understanding of the sensitivity of particle detectors, specifically that they can detect patterns of large-scale anisotropy accurately, even in cases where the sources or the distribution of sources are not clearly identified. The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated precise measurements of the nuclear modification factor, obtained by dividing charged particle yields from heavy ion collisions by their proton-proton counterparts in various centrality ranges and rapidity intervals. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a notable variation in the nuclear modification factor with transverse momentum, showing a more pronounced trend in more peripheral collisions. At a low momentum of around 0.8 GeV, the data indicate that the suppression of high-rapidity particles is more pronounced than for those in medium rapidity. Additionally, this analysis provides evidence of the increase in the number of particles produced as the collision becomes less central, in line with expectations based on the geometric interpretation of heavy ion collisions. A landmark finding of this analysis is the identification of a notable turn-up in the nuclear modification factor at high momentum values, and this effect is more pronounced in more peripheral collisions. Various controls and checks confirm the validity of these measurements; consequently, these results are anticipated to significantly impact the interpretation of data generated during heavy ion and proton-proton runs collected by the ATLAS detector. Furthermore, they are expected to have a profound impact on the development of theories aiming to explain the properties of quark-gluon plasma. High-statistics data coupled with a precise understanding of the detector's performance allow for narrow bin size measurements, and this level of accuracy is expected to be maintained in future runs. Moreover, these results demonstrate the capability of the ATLAS detector to collect high-quality data during heavy ion and proton-proton runs, a level of performance that will be consistent with the higher luminosity forecasts for the LHC at its upgraded 13 TeV centre of mass energy. Consequently, this detector will be well-equipped to accurately investigate the unique features of heavy ion collisions and make precise comparisons with proton-proton collisions at the upgraded LHC. Furthermore, it is expected that this level of performance will be maintained in future runs, allowing researchers to deeply explore the properties of an extreme state of heavy ion collisions, namely quark-gluon plasma. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This concept was successfully validated through actual underwater field trials. To visually grasp the phenomenon of burst-error propagation, a simulated model was developed and demonstrated through no less than three diverse fiber-optic communications scenarios. These simulations showed that the proposed WDFE-MLSE scheme offers superior performance in comparison to other equalization methods. As this technique employs a relatively straightforward architecture, it is more than capable of withstanding high data rates. Moreover, it presents an extremely viable solution for counteracting the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in communications systems. To further comprehend the implications of this technique, a comprehensive analytical model was developed, alongside with an end-to-end simulation model that is capable of evaluating the performance of this technique in real-world applications. This work presents novel insights into the behavior of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications and proposes an ideal technique for counteracting this phenomenon, ultimately positioning this technology as a strong candidate to overcome the limitations posed by dispersion in fiber-optic communications systems. To expand the scope of this research, a novel technique was developed to create custom-made underwater cables that compensate for chromatic dispersion, alongside with a new modulation classification approach that is both accurate and efficient. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method boasts flexibility, allowing it to integrate with TCN's causal convolution operation, and even enable dilation optimization for other temporal recurrence models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on diverse time-series learning tasks, including human activity recognition, physiological signal classification, and financial time-series forecasting. Our optimized models outperform the state-of-the-art in certain tasks and achieve comparable results on others, showcasing the potential of this method to enhance TCN performance across a wide range of applications. The proposed method is available as an open-source framework called Pruning In Time (PIT). It allows users to explore the vast design space of TCN models through a series of experiments, seamlessly integrating with popular deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow. The PIT framework provides a straightforward API for defining custom search spaces that can be optimized for various objective functions, such as model size, latency, and accuracy. We've incorporated a range of pre-defined search spaces that can be executed using the method's user-friendly command-line interface. The Pit framework can be found at https://github.com/author-name/pruning-in-time. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been cross-checked with two separate methods, agree with previous observations from lower-energy collisions and provide support for an idea known as viscous fluid dynamics. Furthermore, these results suggest that the properties of the medium created in these collisions remain the same regardless of the collision energy of 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV. In more central collisions and at the higher momentum level of 2 GeV/c, these fluctuations reach levels that indicate small differences (about 1.5 times) from a constant value known as elliptic viscosity, whose value is 0.072. This understanding of viscosity and the behavior of particles in these collisions could offer valuable insights into improvements of theoretical models and potentially contribute to a greater knowledge of the state of matter in these collisions. Furthermore, extracting these fluctuations in a reliable way allows for a more precise determination of a key property of the medium, known as elliptic viscosity. It also enables researchers to investigate fluctuations in the magnitude of particle flow at different centralities and collisions. Additionally, a notable property of these results is the agreement found between two separate methods used for calculating one of these fluctuations. This agreement led to further confirmation of the reliability of these results and contributes to a better comparison of collision data at the two available energies of 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV. It is also worth noting that studying these results could lead to a greater understanding of how the state of matter in these collisions holds constant across different energies, at least in the range of 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. The most notable aspect of our solution is the absence of a preferred repair, which aligns with the spirit of open-world assumptions. Finally, an overview of our work's potential extension to address additional challenges and a glimpse into a prototype implementation of our framework are also presented. The prototype is designed to handle simple queries and data sets, and future directions for both our research and the prototype are discussed. The prototype's source code is available for reference. The primary focus of this research is on theoretical advancements, although a practical implementation of our approach is also explored. The prototype's limited scope is intentional and serves as the starting point for further development. The most significant challenge in developing the prototype was integrating a consistent and efficient algorithm for evaluating queries. This experience has valuable implications for any future consideration of our research in the context of the semantic web. The web is renowned for its dynamic nature, which could potentially pose data consistency issues. Before closing, some preliminary findings related to data quality are presented, which provide an initial answer to a pressing question raised in this research. The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Moreover, ripples of the influence of the SiD design can be seen extending into other detector designs. As such, we believe that strong research and development participation in the various SiD projects will be beneficial for the broader particle physics community. Finally, we will outline the key performance characteristics of the upgraded SiD and its upgraded components. Furthermore, we will discuss the relevance of the SiD's design to other detector platforms. Lastly, we will touch on the importance of prototyping and the need for close collaboration between experimental physicists, engineers, and technical experts. This review is intended for all members of the SiD community, as well as anyone with an interest in the SiD's design, research into new detector technologies, and particle physics in general. It is also open to feedback and contributions from any parties with involvement or interest in the SiD. In conclusion, we would like to express our gratitude to the organizers for giving us the chance to present our work at the 12th International Conference on Particle Therapy (ICPT) in Heidelberg, Germany, even though it was presented in a virtual format. This review of the SiD Detector has been submitted to the ICPT proceedings. It contains original content not previously published elsewhere. It is available for public access at the ICPT website. Finally, we would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the significant contributions made by our colleague, John Jared, to this review, particularly his input regarding the detector's trigger system. Unfortunately, Jared passed away unexpectedly in 2021, leaving behind a legacy of his scientific achievements and the impact he had on the particle physics community. within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained

0.3 milliHartree. Furthermore, the eCPNN framework facilitates efficient electron
correlation modeling, enabling rapid density and momentum density analysis, as well
as tailored potential function adaptation. By embodying the spirit of machine
learning 'explainability', the eCPNN framework provides a unique glimpse into the
electronic correlation structure of atoms through its density-driven design. Consequently,
this approach provides a compelling pathway for a de facto unification of FCI and
density functional theories. Ultimately, this scheme may serve as a foundational
model for incorporating electron correlation knowledge into density functional
theories. We anticipate this approach to learn electron correlations to be a
groundbreaking step with far-reaching implications. However, a more detailed

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A detailed analysis of the pressures within the formed cavity throughout the surface-seal stage, along with relevant photographs, is also included. Moreover, this study provides a framework for classifying water-entry regimes, including surface seal, partial-seal, and partial-pinching modes. A comprehensive understanding of these findings could be useful for optimizing the performance of various spherical objects moving through water, such as marine vehicles or diving equipment. A significant implication of this research is that at mid-range speeds, the surface-seal regime provides the best conditions for those applications that benefit from maximum pressure within the formed cavity. This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs.

Ultimately, our innovative device design offers a viable solution to overcome the inherent security vulnerabilities in mobile devices and the persistent cyber threats they face.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results show that FPG yields better performance than both non-robust methods and a semi-optimistic reinforcement learning approach. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing complex tasks. We also outline potential applications involving SPCCSs in quantum communication systems and propose the use of optical homodyne tomography for reconstructing these states. SPCCSs can be generated using a different approach involving the application of a parametric amplifying transformation and a beam-spline transformation, both of which yield equivalent success probabilities. These considerations provide a foundation for exploring the execution of complex quantum tasks and the development of quantum metrology applications. Ultimately, producing SPCCSs via these methods paves the way for investigating the catalytic generation of multiple-photon catalyzed coherent states. In such cases, the interaction between a coherent state and a single-photon state is mediated by a beam splitter or parametric amplifier, resulting in the creation of a SPCCS. This transformation can be represented by an amplification transformation, which serves as the inverse of a beam-spline transformation. We examine the properties of these states as a function of the number of photons n. When n = 1, the resulting state is a single-photon state, while larger values of n yield multiple-photon catalyzed coherent states. These states exhibit increased success probabilities with the detection of a photon in a specific output channel. We demonstrate that these states possess a wide range of non-classical behavior, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. In addition, we find that the squeezing in these states varies depending on the number of photons n and the type of catalytic device used. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their application to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to desired values. Our solution employed an implicit collocation method using a non-linear solver, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in finding an optimal solution compared to other methods. We also examine the role of precision in the solver in estimating patient respiratory rates. Our case study illustrates the potential of advanced optimization techniques to tackle complex challenges in dynamic systems. However, we acknowledge the limitations imposed by the requirement for explicit function representations and adequate differentiability, which future research should aim to address. Our approach is representative of the general direction of modern optimization methodologies, and we anticipate that direct approaches will continue to play a key role in future applications. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of collaborative efforts between control engineers and other professionals in addressing real-world problems and the need for open-source software in this field. Our study also highlights the importance of testing and validation in the development of advanced optimization methods, as well as the need to move beyond theoretical applications and instead tackle concrete, real-world challenges. Finally, we emphasize the value of sharing knowledge and expertise within this area and the need for a new generation of control engineers to be trained in the use of these methods. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing re-drilling costs necessitate real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. The method is also robust against data outliers that was demonstrated with an additional scenario. The proposed approach is currently in use by an oil company for real-time geosteering. The fast convergence of this method also allows it to operate on historical well data, providing valuable information on the uncertainty of formation evaluations along with potential applications in flag layer detection and move directions recommendations. The incorporation of this method in a real-time system is discussed along with several move direction recommendations issued during actual real-time geosteering using this approach. The results from this implementation confirm that fast formation evaluations combined with uncertainty quantification can lead to reliable move direction recommendations in real-time geosteering. The proposed approach has also been integrated into an online database of petrophysical property estimations and related uncertainties for all the layers within the well depth range, enabling rapid formation evaluation on demand. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable or better performance on the SIGHAN corpus compared to specialized nested NER models while being applicable to any NER corpus. The proposed approach is particularly useful for adapting models to multiple corpora and reducing the need for retraining different models for each corpus. Human-generated image captions are utilized to train machine learning models to automatically produce descriptive text. These trained models are then leveraged in substantial-scale, real-world applications. Yet, it's been observed that these models can yield inconsistent results, with some generating high-quality text and others producing inaccurate or nonsensical output. This phenomenon suggests that relying solely on human reference data may be insufficient, as it doesn't account for the diversity of system performances. In response, we propose a more comprehensive approach that acknowledges the coexistence of advanced and underdeveloped models in the training dataset. Instead of focusing on a single idealized standard, we adopt a more flexible methodology, combining quantitative assessment with qualitative evaluations using human reference data. This approach allows us to utilize a reduced set of complex, high-quality human-generated captions to guide our models' performance. This methodology is illustrated through our findings from conducting a crowdsourced evaluation of automatic image captions using Google's Cloud Vision API. The data collected during this evaluation is also made available for public use. Ultimately, our results highlight the importance of incorporating diverse human-generated captions that reflect the capabilities of advanced systems, in order to develop more effective automatic image description methods. In particular, we observed that incorporating complex, high-quality human-generated captions along with simpler, lower-quality ones led to a notable improvement in our evaluation results. This suggests that using a single standard for quality might result in overlooking the progress made in recent years. In the context of cloud services, this means that using machine learning models that perform below par on easy cases can still be beneficial if they excel at harder ones. This finding holds implications for other applications that rely on machine learning models and their performance on difficult cases. In the field of automatic image captioning, this means that models should be evaluated on their ability to accurately describe the contents of images, especially those with multiple entities. In the case study presented, we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models like Attention-based Sequence-to-Sequence, can perform subpar when compared to optical character recognition. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Our study highlights the enduring effect of The Big Sort on contemporary American society and suggests that reducing inter-regional misinformation dissemination disparities will require strategies addressing these persistent cultural and personality differences. High-diligence individuals are advised to avoid engaging with misinformation on sensitive topics with people from areas where the population norms diverge from their own, a tactic that could impede dissemination in those regions. Finally, modifying information transmission networks by encouraging Reddit users to interact with content from news sources they hold credible can also be an effective strategy in combating the spread of misinformation. This approach may also improve information diversity within each state. In conclusion, our research underscores the significance of The Big Sort in online misinformation dissemination, a phenomenon that needs to be addressed in social media mitigation strategies. It also highlights opportunities to develop targeted solutions that account for varying cultural and personality conditions across different geographic regions. Furthermore, our results emphasize the value of open-data platforms like Reddit in studying online misinformation dissemination and circulating ideas among diverse population groups. Ultimately, combatting this issue will necessitate a multidisciplinary approach that incorporates insights from physics-based network models, social psychology, sociology, politics, and economics. We hope that our study will pave the way for further research into the complex factors underlying online misinformation dissemination. In addition to providing guidelines for mitigating the spread of misinformation, we hope that our results will stimulate a deeper examination of the underlying factors contributing to this issue, along with the role that internet platforms play in facilitating the circulation of information among diverse population groups in the United States. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. To further explore these findings, a more comprehensive analysis of speech content was conducted using three additional dimensions: hand position, tool vs. environment interaction, and movement speed. To make the results more accessible to the broader robotics community, these findings can be incorporated into a demonstration dataset with enriched auditory and visual features, available for download at https://sites.google.com/eng.cmu.edu/teaching-robotics-by-demonstration. This dataset includes various types of manipulation tasks demonstrated by multiple human instructors using spoken language for guidance. Understanding the complex relationship between speech patterns and instructional intentions represented in this dataset can contribute to developing more effective robotic learning algorithms based on demonstration and speech recognition technology. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/TM-w-monolingual.

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average calculations for calculating prototypes are hindered by their limited representation ability. This paper proposes an innovative framework that extracts unique prototypes for each class by combining feature extraction and prototype calculation as a single optimization problem. The proposed framework learns class-specific prototypes by sharing information across support sets and using a prototype extraction module that adheres to the norm of a mixture model. This module minimizes the discrepancy between the distribution of features within a class and the distribution of prototypes. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework surpasses average-based methods and achieves comparable performance to memory-based methods on datasets such as miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain datasets, without the need to store additional memory. Moreover, our framework outperforms the state of the art on zero-shot learning benchmarks without any modifications. The code for this paper is available on https://github.com/zwang84/prototyping. Additionally, a pre-trained model can be found on https://github.com/zwang84/zero-shot-learning.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The source code of the proposed MSDCR framework is available at https://github.com/ASUS-AILab/MSDCR. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. This new estimator's magnitude dispersion at $z = 1.2$ is $0.22$ ($1\sigma$) or $0.36$ ($2\sigma$) in magnitude. Moreover, we discovered that using this estimator in place of the standard approach leads to a finding of a non-zero cosmological constant with a $2.9\sigma$ significance level. A simplified model of lensing SN Ia, which takes into account the effects of lensing and the intrinsic properties of Type Ia supernovae, is sufficient for these surveys. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we present evidence that the nearest neighbor configuration of oxygen atoms plays a crucial role in determining the spin lifetimes, and are confident that with further development of this technology, we can achieve long electronic spin lifetimes in these defect centers. Our work lays the foundation for the exploration of large-scale photonic silicon systems that integrate solid-state interfaces with optical spins. By combining the high density T centers located near the interface with the unique properties of silicon photonic materials, we aim to establish a new framework for quantum communication technology. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This work paves the way for a broader exploration of non-equilibrium multiagent learning with rational behavior in various application domains. Ultimately, it highlights the significance of developing suitable game models that accommodate rational player behavior via learning under uncertainty. Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. Consequently, this partnership of calculations allows us to derive a generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation directly from the superbosonization formula. This equivalence also enables us to investigate various bosonization strategies, including the application of these methods to complex matrices and non-degenerate mass parameters. Lastly, we explore ways to further generalize these strategies, likely enabling the solution of pending technical issues. With these advancements, the supersymmetry method now holds significant promise in tackling a broad range of quantum field theory and matrix model challenges. Furthermore, our work indicates that these strategies may also be relevant to exploring the fundamental connections between partition functions in physics and the study of planar graphs. Ultimately, our findings provide a new framework that likely enables the extension of the supersymmetry method to a wide range of matrix models and field theories, likely playing a crucial role in resolving several outstanding issues. proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental

enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases.

which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44.

top quark polarization analysis is presented.

CTEV analysis stage, with a combined 32 fb^-1 of luminosity.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also show that the imaginary surfaces derived from these connections exhibit domain growth similar to that driven by analytic continuations of the Riemann surface of the Toda equation. Additionally, we discuss potential connections to the MacKay-Tweedale duality in the Dyson model.

These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple temporal dynamics. Such behavior holds universally across any lattice structure; however, its impact is particularly noticeable in triangular and diamond arrangements. Here, in such environments, self-organizing pairs exhibit a unique kind of synchronized movement, emulating a motion akin to their movement within a Kagome lattice and Lieb lattice, respectively. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. As a result, a substantial proportion of the putative black holes in the Galactic center may actually be neutron star binaries that have been mistakenly identified, due to their low outburst rates. This also implies that a substantial number of neutron star binaries have been incorrectly accounted for in the Galactic population, specifically within the Galactic center. This underestimation has a relatively small impact on the overall population of neutron star binaries in the region; however, it does exceed the total number of radio pulsars discovered there. Overall, it is estimated that approximately 15-20% of the variables X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center can be expected to exhibit outbursts in the next decade. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The revised framework's potential for addressing other memory constraint learning challenges is also discussed. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields Fq, the total residue map natural to the toric fixed field of a smooth absolute value on the algebraic closure of Fq, uniquely determines the non-trivial absolute values on this field up to isomorphism. This note provides a broader context for this phenomenon by establishing that a similar situation applies to all finite extensions of non-archimedean absolute value systems on algebraically closed fields. This theoretical framework facilitates a proof that up to isomorphism, the toric fixed fields of non-archimedean absolute value systems on algebraically closed fields have a countable set of realisations. This result further enables us to demonstrate that the set of absolute value systems on an algebraically closed field, once we move to its non-trivial realisations and ignoring isomorphisms, is also countable. This countability of absolute value systems is also explicitly utilised in our proofs of two theorems. Firstly, we prove that the combination of continuous automorphisms and the total residue map on the algebraic closure of Fq, extended to its non-trivial realisations, form a dense set in the space of continuous automorphisms. Secondly, we demonstrate that the same principle applies to the power series fields over algebraically closed fields. This result is particularly showcased by the fact that over a field with an infinite cardinality, the power series fields over it have a countable set of realisations. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, this design is adaptable for future detectors like third-generation detectors and gravitational wave detectors employing laser power recycling and multi-stage amplification.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and true language representations, allowing for a start-from-the-basics approach and mitigating the difficulty of sequential generation. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid $n$-gram residual neural model achieves superior performance at a lower cost, often surpassing state-of-the-art baselines by a substantial margin - up to 2.03 times better in terms of BLEU score. Moreover, our method exhibits exceptional robustness to hyperparameter changes and a remarkable ability to generalize across diverse tasks with $n$-gram codebook representations. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramResidual. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our method achieves notable success in face reconstruction from real-world images, demonstrating a unique ability to accommodate head poses ranging from 0 to 60 degrees with minimal deviation. This is particularly evident in cases where certain face points exhibit little pose variation, as seen in front-facing images, but also in scenarios with significant pose variation, as seen in images depicting larger head orientations. This implies our model's capability to effectively capture pose information, in addition to occlusion. We also examine the occlusion aspect of our model and find that it effectively identifies and ignores superfluous face parts created through face replication, in effect treating them as occluded areas. This understanding of our model's behavior in dealing with complex real-world images suggests several potential future extensions to the network architecture. This includes exploring other techniques that employ multi-task learning to manage both pose and occlusion, as well as examining the broader applicability of this method to three-dimensional alignment and enhancement of non-face objects, such as hands and ears. This could be accomplished by incorporating additional information about these objects through supplementary training datasets. This line of thinking also raises inquiries regarding the model's ability to detect a wide range of occlusions, from those that are subtle to those that are quite apparent, as well as its potential to handle more complex situations with multiple areas of occlusion. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Notably, this study demonstrates that even inadequate WSD models can achieve superior performance to renowned baselines when utilizing highly efficient word sense representations.  Furthermore, the model's performance continues to improve over time, demonstrating its potential in addressing real-world applications.  The proposed approach is made available for public access on GitHub.  Future directions for both WSD and data augmentation in natural language processing are also discussed.  In particular, the paper explores several intriguing questions regarding the integration of structured knowledge and augmented data, which could facilitate breakthroughs in complex NLP tasks.  A new benchmark designed to evaluate the incorporation of structured knowledge in natural language processing models is introduced.  This includes a set of context-gloss pairs created to assess their ability to recognize the same sense of a polysemous word in various contexts.  The model's performance is monitored at regular intervals and the results are presented in the form of a ranking that highlights the progression of each approach over time.  A unique aspect of this study involves the development of multiple new techniques for combining structured knowledge and augmented data.  These techniques involve various methods of redefining the context and the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base.  A data-driven approach is used to identify the most effective way to combine knowledge about a word's different senses.  The paper's contributions are comprehensive, with significant advancements in the application of deep learning models in natural language processing tasks.  These contributions note the models' reliance on large datasets of labeled examples, the challenge of scaling to multiple word senses, and the importance of incorporating structured knowledge in models' training. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This discovery paves the way for further studies of heavy quark production in proton-nucleus collisions and the potential to probe nuclear matter with high-energy protons. Details of the analysis as well as additional results are presented in this report. In particular, a minimum cross-sectional area of 2.37 micro barns for gold nuclei was determined by extrapolating to the light-cone wavelength of the gold nucleus and a minimum hard-parton cross-sectional area of 1.12 micro barns was found at a transverse momentum of 600 GeV for quarks and 770 GeV for gluons. In addition, the data revealed evidence at the two-standard-deviation level for the production of single top quarks in excess of background predictions, with a cross-sectional area of 26 nanobarns ± 15 nanobarns. Further investigation is needed to confirm this result due to the presence of potential contamination from top quark pair production and limitations in reconstructing single top quark events. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. To evaluate this method, we develop a dataset based on public music datasets and gather crowd-sourced feedback to compare our approach's performance against other metadata options. Our results suggest that our music captioning model not only outperforms alternative methods but also demonstrates relevance to real-world applications. Moreover, we showcase the method's practical usefulness by integrating it into a practical application. This involves releasing an open-source Python framework that other platforms can adapt for their own music playlist descriptions. This framework's effectiveness is evident to a degree, as demonstrated through a case study of the Apple Music playlists. Interestingly, our findings indicate that while our model excels in overall performance, it can struggle with certain song interpretations. To address this limitation, we introduce a supplementary method called cross-training, which aims to enhance the model's ability to process a wider range of music genres. This method's potential benefits are illustrated through a dataset expansion example. Lastly, we explore potential directions for further improving music captioning, including the integration of external metadata and the development of a specialized model architecture. This includes a detailed explanation of why pre-trained models might not always be the most suitable choice for this task. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting the potential applications and future directions for this approach in the context of music recommendation and beyond. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional results on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin. Notably, DCAN has shown substantial improvement over simplified versions, indicating the importance of modeling context at both action boundary and proposal levels. Moreover, our findings suggest that existing boundary matching methods can be enhanced through the incorporation of context aggregation. We have found that densely generated proposals with semantic distinctness can be achieved by setting a minimal overlap between proposals. This has resulted in our method attaining top performance on THUMOS-14, where actions are detected with high accuracy at the frame level. Overall, our approach has set a new performance bar for temporal action detection, especially under the strict setting. Moreover, our method has demonstrated exceptional robustness and flexibility, extending favorably to activity detection. On ActivityNet v1.3, our approach has detected over 50% of activities with high accuracy at the frame level, outperforming all current methods. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. The study also assesses its cooperative and non-cooperative performance in dynamic scenarios. Introduction Dynamic potential fields have been widely used to guide mobile robots toward target locations while avoiding collisions with other mobile robots and stationary objects. This approach relies on assigning each entity a specific potential field to dictate the robot's movement. While simple and effective, this method faces two significant challenges: first, creating potential fields that prevent the occurrence of local minima; second, ensuring that non-cooperative robots behave rationally. To address these issues, this paper proposes a collision avoidance algorithm that utilizes a dynamic vortex potential field and its gradient to create cooperative behavior between mobile robots.
