Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The proposed approach achieves superior results by combining optimal performance with satisfactory reproducibility and significantly aids the process of tuning natural language processing models by leading to substantial improvements in overall model performance. The proposed method's advantages are further highlighted by a comparative analysis of various NLP models that showcase the approach's beneficial impact on model selection. In particular, the proposed method yields optimal results across nine out of ten evaluation metrics, serving as a clear indicator of its effectiveness. One potential limitation of this study is the observed increase in required computational resources when employing the j-k fold CV method, although this expense is considered a worthwhile investment in achieving superior model performance. In conclusion, introducing the j-k fold CV method provides a valuable framework for tuning natural language processing models that prioritizes variance reduction over bias, recommended for any research team exploring this type of model. Finally, extending this approach to additional machine learning tasks is advised and is currently being investigated. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. In addition, this method allows for the creation of motion-compensated images using only a short-encoded data set, which is beneficial in reducing scan time. It is particularly effective in imaging the heart and lymph nodes, and may be beneficial in imaging other moving organs and body structures. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Interestingly, it reveals that forming an ICCBF becomes essentially equivalent to solving a Most Primitive Reachable State problem, a new benchmark with substantial implications. These innovations have the potential to liberally combine various control strategies, such as feedback linearization and discrete log-barriers, in a single, unified framework called Combined Control Barriers. This framework is then successfully applied to a challenging aerospace scenario. With its development, the field of Control Barrier Functions can now tackle any system that can be reduced to a form suitable for optimization over a manifold. Nevertheless, the excitement is short-lived as a counterexample arises, showing that this capability is only achievable at the theoretical level and cannot be realized through actual computation. Consequently, this discovery results in a major revision of the approach presented in the initial version of this paper. In response to a question regarding higher order base systems, the paper outlines two potential solutions but stops short of providing a complete answer, leaving it as an open issue. Furthermore, it failed to address issues related to persistent navigation in the presence of disturbances, only to have these shortcomings pointed out in a critique, which in turn led to a persistence of a particular solution. Notably, the approach presented in this paper for solving discrete log-barriers via backtracking was previously considered the state-of-the-art but has since been superseded. Despite these limitations, the paper remains a significant contribution to the field of control theory, especially in relation to its application in spacecraft rendezvous. In the words of its authors, "the best way to deal with people who do not understand a different language is to speak a common language such as mathematics." This paper speaks this common language known as mathematics with authority and a clear command of the language known as the theory of control barrier functions. This theory is an innovative approach to solving complex control problems by redefining the control objective in terms of a safety function, with each subsequent layer defined in a higher dimension

Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This new model, which incorporates a conservation principle for angular momentum, develops a formalism that views the common envelope as a rossiter-mcclintock effect on a shrinking orbit. This formalism makes it possible to accurately predict the outcome of these interactions, including both mergers and further binary interactions. This new model also provides a clearer physical understanding of the common envelope phase, especially in terms of how it affects the motion of stars and the behavior of their envelopes, based on a detailed analysis of all the conservation laws that apply, including those of linear momentum, angular momentum, and energy. This formalism also makes it possible to accurately account for the effects of surface free fall on both the linear momentum and energy of the system, as well as identifying the key parameters that govern the behavior of common envelope phases, particularly in multiple star systems, where all the stars play a crucial role in determining the outcome of these interactions. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted signatures, such as four bottom jets with at least one Higgs decay channel to leptons or photons, and estimate the background contributions. We also examine the sensitivity of these colliders to distinct configurations of the two leading HEFT coefficients in the double Higgs production process. Finally, we highlight that in the low-energy regime, the cross-section of the subprocess $WW \to HH$ is highly sensitive to the coefficient governing a new Higgs self-interaction, and that at the planned collider operating at 1 TeV, this sensitivity can be as precise as a 10\% reduction in the self-interaction strength at 1$\sigma$ confidence level with 1 ab$^{-1}$ at 1 TeV, corresponding to a 3$\sigma$ discovery threshold at 350 fb$^{-1}$. We conclude by outlining some promising avenues for further optimization of the double Higgs production analysis at the two planned colliders. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas surface density. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the mass of new star formation, indicating a limit on the efficiency of star formation due to the available gas. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. To facilitate adoption, we have open-sourced BoAnon at https://github.com/ucb-bar/boanon. This framework can also be adapted to other optimization tasks requiring structural information. Consequently, BoAnon acts as a foundation for our next research initiative, which involves incorporating external expertise into the optimization process. By integrating various learning algorithms with BoAnon's contextual structure learning, we aim to unlock its full potential for the auto-tuning of complex computer systems. Through this work, we have introduced a novel approach to learning the structure of computer systems from logs, their performance models, and dependency information. This method, based on contextual structure learning, has successfully accelerated the optimization of hardware architecture search for energy-latency objectives by a factor of 5-7x. This achievement has piqued the interest of other researchers in the field, leading to an opportunity to collaborate and build upon this work. Our current research initiative with Microsoft Research involves exploring multiple machine learning algorithms to enhance the structure learning process. By integrating various learning methods with our BoAnon framework, we aim to further improve its performance and make it even more effective at optimizing complex computer systems. This experience has also taught us the value of open-source collaboration, as our work with UC Berkeley has shown. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ucb-bar

As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$,

production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with

density clumps in these environments can form massive ($10-300M_{\odot}$) dust
envelopes on a timescale compatible with dust detected in external galaxies. It

dust grains into superlarge dust particles, with potential to provide dust

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our approach has the potential to enhance the practical application of far-field 3D detection in self-driving vehicles. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The data collected during the 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES include high precision radial velocity measurements, stellar spectroscopic data from the TESS and Kepler missions, as well as information on the planets and host stars derived from literature sources and the Planetary Systems Cross-Match (PSCM) database. The target selection algorithm used for the survey is based on a set of predefined criteria, which included prioritizing planets with compositions that could be analyzed with the JWST, systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The survey's primary objectives will be investigated with the high precision radial velocity measurements, while the stellar spectroscopic data are suitable for further magnetic field, stellar activity, and stellar mass analyses. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. This opposition to topological compactness characterizes such groups' actions, and as a result, we conclude that none of these groups are topologically compact when their base space is a locally compact, non-compact space. This conclusion also holds for groups whose action is effectively transitive. Ultimately, on compact spaces, we establish that none of these groups are precompact. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Using the field MUSS stars, a mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood was defined through a process involving Gaussian Process regression. The resulting data show a distinct feature in the GP derivative, located at approximately 0.337 ± 0.013 to 0.026 M_(? ̇_odot) mass units, which indicates where the M-dwarf sample transitions from being fully convective in its interior to partly convective. This study presents a novel approach to calibrating low-mass stars using a comprehensive Bayesian framework and accurately determines the mass range for these stars through sophisticated regression tools. Further research with this sample will be continued in future papers. Additionally, the method developed in this paper can be applied to any new low-mass star spectrum obtained across different surveys. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures. 
A finite element method simulation of the proposed design revealed that the line waves produced can operate in the range from 0.8 to 4.5 THz, allowing for adjustable wavelengths between 0.26 and 1.4 cm.
The localized field enhancements presented can exceed 10 times the amplitude of the incident field. 
A theoretical model of the proposed design also predicts that the line waves produced can operate in the range from 1.3 to 10.2 μm, enabling adjustable wavelengths between 1.03 to 6.56 μm.

A simple structure composed of a patch made from biased n-doped semiconductor material, situated between two negative resistance layers, also supports line waves.

In contrast, the proposed graphene patch structure offers several improvements over this type of structure.
While the line waves produced in both types of structures exhibit similar properties, the proposed graphene patch structure supports line waves in the optical range.

Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries with respect to efficiency, this study provides an in-depth analysis and illustrates potential enumeration strategies using self-joins. These advancements lead to more complex proof of intractability in comparison to queries without self-joins. Additionally, this study introduces an existing method to prove intractability in the presence of self-joins and sets criteria for both feasible and infeasible queries with limited complexity, providing answers for low-arity queries and those with cyclic patterns. However, many cases remain unclear. Definitions of cyclic and acyclic queries are also reviewed in this investigation. Finally, a way to incorporate other database operations into query evaluation is also demonstrated. This study hopes to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of database query evaluation complexity. Learn more about this topic in this video presentation. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. A corresponding Turing machine can be a two-way transducer that operates in a limited context and is shown to be equivalent to a specific type of MSO-transducer with reference to context, preserving both their computability and non-computability. 

On the theoretical side, this research also involves establishing a fundamental connection between continuous functions and the properties of regular languages under a specific operation, as well as demonstrating that this relationship holds for both rational and regular functions. 

Finally, to demonstrate the practical usefulness of these results, a case study is presented showing how they can be applied to a specific problem related to the synthesis of reactive systems. 

The approach developed in this research relies heavily on a specific decision-making component related to whether a specific pattern appears in an infinite string with a specific prefix-dependent context, and this is the basis for most of the results presented. 

One of the most significant outcomes of this research is the definition of a specific class of functions that can be computed by a specific type of transducer and is equivalent to the intersection of two regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to resolve the synthesis problem for a specific type of reactive system specified using automata with parameter-dependent acceptability conditions.

This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've also introduced a Cauchy-type variant of this method, which provides a way to initialize and converge to the solution by starting with an initial state that is further from the origin than the reachable state space. We've tested these methods on a linear system and a nonlinear rotor control system. 

In the case of the linear system, the method converges to the solution provided by the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. For the rotor control system, which has a stiff dynamics, the Cauchy-type variant was found to be more efficient in terms of computational time and iterations than the standard successive sweep method. The Cauchy-type variant initialized with a state that was twice as far from the origin as the reachable state space reached the solution in 17 iterations compared to 50 iterations for the standard method. 

The paper also presents a dynamic domain decomposition approach for solving large-scale Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations by dividing the state space into subdomains and solving for the smallest subdomain first. This method assumes that the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation has a continuous and smooth solution.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell

In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.

spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he posed the question whether $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/ \log y)$ would always hold for any y such that $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$, even under the condition where RH is true. We prove that in cases where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ except for very small values close to the critical value, $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ and that it fails infinitely many times when RH is not true. 

Our new estimates and our derivation for the count of y-friable integers for any y such that $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ also raises questions as to whether this relationship might hold only when $y$ is far away from $x$. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. 
Despite limitations like relying on expensive pre-trained models for retrieval and potential biases in using existing data, our work lays the foundation for exploring low-density retrieval methods and incorporating diverse data sets to enhance cross-task generalization.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is hosted on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/EdgardoCM/Hyperparameter Optimization for Private Deep Learning. The paper also presents a comprehensive survey on hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, and is an extension of our previous conference paper presented at the 12th IEEE International Conference on Cloud Computing. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a robotic system has been trained using a variety of noisy feedback types. Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. The research suggests that a combination of personality traits and sensation seeking is key to predicting drug consumption for the pleiades around cannabis, LSD, and volatile substance abuse. Interestingly, impulse control was not a significant factor in classifying users of the substances considered in this study. The research underlines the value of large data sets and advanced analytical techniques in improving the accuracy of drug consumption risk evaluation. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  We have also introduced an evaluation framework that incorporates human-generated examples and showcases the diversity of ATOMIC by highlighting key differences between its contents and a rival dataset.  This dataset is unique due to its extensive nature, covering nearly a million instances of these types of rules and is available for download at https://github.com/ygong91/atomic. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The conditioned random walk formulation enables us to leverage established limits from exchangeable fragment processes, while considering the initial conditions enables us to establish rate bounds and limit theorems. The methods developed in this work can be applied to derive analogous results for other exchangeable fragment processes. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications. These findings provide a fundamental understanding of photonic quantum information processing and enable the development of complex photonic systems with tailored interactions between modes. Furthermore, a 1D photonic lattice was designed to exhibit a desired mode coupling phenomenon and this demonstration paves the way for implementing photonic versions of boson accumulation and other collective quantum phenomena. Optical parametric amplification was also successfully achieved in a triple-well structure, further highlighting the capabilities of these custom-made photonic structures. These developments hold significant potential for incorporating mode coupling and other multi-mode interactions in photonic integrated circuits, enabling a wide range of applications including quantum communication, metrology and cryptography. Furthermore, we show that fano resonances which result from inter-orbital coupling can be utilized for enobase distinction, a critical function that could be employed for quantum accoutrement processing, a concept inspired by digital computing but involving variables with multiple degrees of freedom. Finally, we explore the possibility of scaling our photonic systems to the multi-mode quantum regime by examining the two-dimensional photonic lattice structure of an atomic ensemble, and demonstrate the ability to control the phase structure of this system using a single beam. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique of writing multi-mode interactions into photonic integrated circuits is accurate to within 100 nm, which is the largest precision achievable with current methods. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Finally, we outline an ideal form for unclonable encryption constructions and propose the term "unclonable encryption" itself. We hope this becomes a focus area in further exploration of quantum cryptography. Thanks to our references, we've been able to build upon prior work by the field's experts, particularly Broadbent and Lord. We aim for this survey to serve as an accessible introduction for those just beginning to study these concepts. We've also included an appendix containing additional security proofs in extended versions of our submissions to TCC 2020 and PQCrypto 2021. We're grateful to Peter Boyle and Tom Stada Fernandes for their valuable feedback in crafting this narrative. We hope this will motivate others to explore the fascinating realm of unclonable encryption. We've made our references freely available to ensure easy access, and we hope this will spark further innovation in this area of quantum cryptography. We're confident that solving the challenges presented in this work will come from combining our collection of constructions, together with input from quantum cryptography experts. Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. Understanding these similarities and differences
will be crucial for answering pending questions concerning planetary evolution and
the potential for life on planets that host close binary stars or experience mass
transfer from accretion during their formation. High-quality observational data and
advancements in computational modeling will jointly contribute to a more in-depth
analysis of the interactions between these celestial bodies and their surroundings.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, we examine the spin-orbit proximity effect in cobalt layers proximate to thin films of bismuth, utilizing a combination of transport and ferromagnetic resonance measurements to gather information. The measured resistivity and ferromagnetic resonance line width suggest the presence of a spin-orbit proximity effect; however, its magnitude falls short of theoretical predictions, likely resulting from scattering at the interface. This hypothesis warrants further investigation, such as high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy, to validate the presence of a spin-orbit field in the cobalt layers and pinpoint the scattering length. Empirical data suggest the cobalt layers' SOPE could be amplified by reducing the Bi layer thickness below 5 nm. This finding implies scattering at the interface plays a significant role in spin-orbit proximity effect and that this effect could be controllable through choice of adjacent material and interface conditions. This knowledge may be of use in designing 2D systems with tailored SOPE to discover new phases in superconductor, semimetallic systems or to enhance the persistence of spin orbits in a nearby layer. A potential risk exists in systems with strong spin-orbit proximity and large scattering lengths, where the persistence of SOPE could lead to malfunctions when the proximity layer is switched from a strong spin-orbit material to one with minimal spin-orbit coupling, such as the case with a gold layer. A gold layer would result in a substantial increase in the resistivity of the ferromagnetic layer, likely rendering it unsuitable for use in spin-torque driven systems. A more detailed analysis of these effects is included in the supplementary materials. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on conventional training methods without considering robust performance against out-of-distribution data, including those encountered in real-world applications with varying patient demographics and pathological conditions. Furthermore, there's a lack of study on the quantitative dose-quantitation (e.g, metabolic rate) improvement concurrent with enhanced image quality. We address these shortcomings by introducing novel uncertainty-aware deep learning techniques that incorporate physical modeling and adaptive data weighting, resulting in enhanced robustness to out-of-distribution data and capability to handle overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methods yield superior performance on PET reconstruction, both subjectively evaluated through quality factor and objectively measured through metabolic rate accuracy, when compared to conventional training and other baseline models. Moreover, our method's ability to handle uncertainty and overfitting allows for reliable performance on unseen data. We have obtained promising results on low-dose PET reconstruction with reduced doses, suggesting its potential utility in clinical settings. Furthermore, we have observed that our proposed method achieves comparable metabolic rate accuracy to conventional training on regular PET scans, indicating its safety for use in those imaging protocols. Comprehensive experimental evaluations have validated the robustness and efficiency of our method on out-of-distribution data, including pathologies and MRI-PET registration protocols that weren't encountered during training. Overall, our proposed uncertainty-aware deep learning approach has demonstrated superior performance and robustness in PET image enhancement from low-dose scans with associated MRI data, particularly with regard to metabolic rate accuracy and robustness to out-of-distribution data. We believe this work has significant implications for lower-dose PET imaging, suggesting that high-quality PET images can be achieved with reduced doses while maintaining metabolic rate accuracy. We have made our model's code publicly available for others to build upon. We have also outlined additional potential research directions for lower-dose PET imaging based on our proposed approach. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, our approach yields a general parameterized algorithm for identifying whether a directed graph allows an upward spanning forest. Additionally, we've explored the general question of parameterized intractability for upward planarity, demonstrating the intractability of several parameters, including the number of sink vertices, treedepth, and the Spathwidth parameter. Building upon these results, we've designed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the Spathwidth parameter. These advancements resolve several open questions and contribute to a better understanding of the upward planarity problem across various graph classes. Finally, we've obtained a general characterization for graph classes that allow an upward spanning forest, leading to a general XP algorithm based on the graph's parameter value. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By combining these strategies, we gain a deeper understanding of the operator growth phenomenon and its underlying connections to quantum field theory. Finally, our research introduces a novel method for calculating Krylov complexity that serves as a benchmark for this phenomenon. Ultimately, we demonstrate that in the realm of quantum field theory, the operator growth hypothesis holds true. Additionally, we identify a fundamental boundary beyond which the hypothesis cannot prevail. We also calculate the complexity of a quantum state and the scaling of entanglement across all Lie-symmetric systems, yielding results that significantly contribute to our knowledge of the operator growth phenomenon. Furthermore, our results obtained from coherent states hold a universal nature, implying that they are not only a property of these states but rather a feature of the underlying Lie-symmetric systems themselves. We also explore the connection between operator growth and entanglement, including the possibility of one causing a change in the other. We observe that in some cases, the operator growth hypothesis is a consequence of the scaling of entanglement. We also identify a situation where the operator growth hypothesis fails to account for the increase in entanglement. Lastly, we establish that the information capacity of the systems we studied is directly related to the operator growth hypothesis. We also demonstrate that in some cases, the operator growth hypothesis results in a situation where the information capacity is infinite, meaning that the system is over the limit where this phenomenon can continue. Ultimately, our research proves that the operator growth hypothesis leads to a situation where the information capacity is always greater than the entanglement, and that together they fall within the information capacity of the system. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Practical solutions to overcome potential beam-RF system limitations are also discussed. Furthermore, the general principles derived from these studies can be applied to other multi-pass particle accelerators. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but leave the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our results highlight the benefits of using EKMP for learning complex human demonstrations, even when the target point is obstructed. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our findings also support the established expectation that in such materials, the critical point without magnetic field should be located at the point of singularity along the doping concentration axis. Direct observation of this transition offers a new testing ground for the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in the complex material structure of cuprates.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Our analysis of 6172 principal components yielded 94 marked deviations 
and 24 distinguished binary prospects, including the known binary asteroid 
(16) Psyche, with additional targets presented as potential wide binary 
candidates. Furthermore, we highlight the capabilities of these detection 
methods to identify non-binary asteroids exhibiting anomalous motion. 
Ultimately, our research provides a groundwork for employing these analytical 
techniques across high-resolution asteroid surveys such as those from Gaia. 
Additionally, we outline an upcoming project, J-Anser, a high-resolution stellar 
anomaly detection system designed for gauging the sensitivity of such surveys. 
J-Anser's future deployment will significantly contribute to discovering more 
wide binary asteroids. Nonetheless, we anticipate a notable portion of the 
designated binary prospects discovered here to be confirmed as such, leading the 
way for a deeper understanding of binary asteroid dynamics and mass distribution. 
On the other hand, if a notable number of detected wide binary prospects end up 
being refuted, it would imply constraints on binary stability, with implications 
on cometary formation theories. Nonetheless, we are confident in our analytical 
approach and Pan-STARRS1 data, and are looking forward to the outcome of this 
discovery along with the detection of additional wide binary asteroids in 
 upcoming projects. Finally, we are also open to enhancing our analytical 
 techniques with machine learning algorithms, particularly those featuring 
 extensibility

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate South American rift system.  They found that pre-break-up extensional and E-W to NE-SW directed shear strains in Central and West Africa corresponded to conjugate S-N directed extensional and shear strains in Southeast Brazil and Northeast Argentina.  This led to the conclusion that the pre-break-up rifts in these regions were oriented at approximately 180 degrees to each other.  As the continents continued to move apart, the Central and West African cratons underwent further extension and thinning, resulting in low-density lithosphodic micro-continents that broke off and sank on the African side.  These micro-continents were paired with the Serra do Saldet high-density craton in Southeast Brazil.  Similarly, in Southeast Brazil and Northeast Argentina, the extensional and shear strains caused pre-break-up extensional and shear strains to deepen and widen pre-break-up rifts, forming sedimentary basins like the Rio Grande do Sul.  Further studies have shown that the pre-break-up rifts in Southeast Brazil and Northeast Argentina experienced post-break-up subsidence and continued to function as sedimentary basins until the Cretaceous period.  Analysis of regional isostasy allowed researchers to model the pre-break-up history of the conjugate South American rift system and the post-break-up evolution of the South Atlantic rift basin.  Their results indicate that the basin's post-break-up evolution was influenced by changes in lithosphodic thickness and the break-off of the African cratons, with the Serra do Saldet high-density craton sinking on the African side.  This led to non-uniform post-break-up subsidence patterns on the African and South American sides of the basin, with potential implications for hydrocarbon exploration in the region.  In particular, the data suggest that the Pre-salt layer on the African side of the basin may be a conjugate feature of the Post-salt layer on the South American side. We propose a new set of parton density functions that depend on the parton's movement direction and/or its virtuality, encompassing functions like parton momentum dependence, parton virtuality, and 'colloidal' partons. These functions are linked to modified parton distribution functions and quark gluon distributions at the leading twist, and they manifest in unmodified form at higher twists. Notably, the 'colloidal' partons' function is connected to the Boer-Mulders function through a parton virtuality factor that governs the transition between them. This relationship enables access to the 'colloidal' partons' function from data related to the Boer-Mulders function. Furthermore, we illustrate how the parton virtuality factor can be extracted from lattice QCD. Our review focuses on identifying potential signatures that could facilitate the experimental discovery of these new functions at relevant scales. Several production processes are considered as potential platforms for detecting these parton density functions with various probes, including lepton pair production, jet production, and dijet production. The relevant scale for each process is determined, and an order-of-magnitude analysis is performed to estimate the relevant mass scales for these processes. This review covers the parton virtuality, 'colloidal', and momentum-dependent partons, as well as the BGW parton density function. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these functions and their constituent partons. It is crucial to note that these parton density functions are not directly linked to the standard parton model, and they require a more complex interpretation in the context of the wave function approach. Furthermore, our order-of-magnitude analysis suggests that the relevant mass scales for these processes are in the range of 1 GeV to over 100 GeV, depending on the parton density function and the production process. This highlights the importance of reconsidering the parton model's basic assumptions in light of these findings. Our review also emphasizes the need for lattice QCD calculations that take into account the parton density functions' dependence on the parton's movement direction and virtuality. This includes lattice QCD's contribution to the determination of the relevant mass scales for these processes. Moreover, our order-of-magnitude analysis has implications for the experimental discovery of these parton density functions, and it highlights the importance of considering all possible production processes and the relevant mass scales for each process. This, in turn, has important consequences for the interpretation of experimental data in light of these parton density functions.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, we demonstrate that the smooth part of the mapping class group of this blowup shares the same cardinality as that of the real line. This theorem is a direct extension to higher dimensions of a key finding from our previous research published in arXiv:2111.03189. Furthermore, we establish that the smooth part of the mapping class group of any symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ will also be infinite. This result is a direct application of a more general theorem regarding the smooth part of the mapping class group of symplectic blowups, which is in turn a direct extension to higher dimensions of a key finding from our previous research published in arXiv:2111.03189. 

In the one-dimensional case, a Kaehler form $\omega$ on $T^1$ is essentially just the standard orientation-induced symplectic form, and it easily satisfies the specified irrationality criterion. Therefore, we are able to determine that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of any blowup of $T^1$ is infinite. This conclusion complements a key finding from our previous research published in arXiv:2111.03189. 

We are also able to demonstrate that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of any blowup of the complex projective space $CP^2$ is finite. This provides a clear answer to a question posed by F. Cano in his thesis. Finally, we offer an arbitrarily large finite genus analog of this result. In addition, we offer a direct extension to any complex dimension $d$ of both of these conclusions. This means that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of any blowup of the complex projective space $CP^d$ is finite, and we offer a direct finite genus analog of this result. Furthermore, we provide a clear answer to a question posed by B. Weitschats in his thesis.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through a universal pseudo-NG field theory framework. This exploration of the anomalous NG theorem has implications for our understanding of solid-state physics, where Lie algebras and groups play a pivotal role in surface science and "unusual" matter phenomena. Moreover, this research has expanded our knowledge of the anomalous NG theorem across both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory contexts. A concise introduction to Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory has been provided to facilitate a broader appreciation of the fundamental principles underlying the anomalous NG theorem. In addition, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra has been shown to emerge universally from the study of Lie algebras in this context. A distinctive feature of our research includes a representation of the anomalous NG theorem using geometric Lie algebras, focusing particularly on an irreducible algebra representing the global anomaly. A profound connection between the anomalous NG theorem and Riemann's distribution theorem has been discovered, offering a glimpse into the deeper mathematical principles underlying this phenomenon. Lastly, an extensive literature review has been conducted on both the theoretical and experimental aspects of the anomalous NG theorem. A unique opportunity for further exploration presents itself in the form of an open problem related to the study of Lie algebras in quantum field theory. A historical context for the discoveries made in this research has been provided, highlighting the key contributions of renowned physicists, from the early breakthroughs of Yukawa and Nambu to the more recent findings of researchers involved in this study. A concise biography of each of these influential scientists has been included. A unique aspect of this research is the presentation of an interactive website

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. High quality Heusler films with this technique also enable the exploration of their magnetic properties. Notably, GdPtSb exhibits a high spin-polarization at room temperature, making it suitable for spintronic applications. High resolution transmission electron microscopy was used to analyze the crystal structure, while first-principles modeling was employed to explain the observed rotations through surface and sub-surface atomic arrangements. This study provides a route to controlled remote epitaxy and potentially other low-coherence processes, enabling the development of unique materials with desired properties. Furthermore, it enables the reuse of expensive substrate materials, reducing environmental waste. Additionally, this research introduces a new method for achieving remote epitaxy, controllable through temperature and graphene cleanliness, which could be adapted to other low-coherence processes. This could potentially allow for the controlled fabrication of unique materials with the desired magnetic and electronic properties throughout the process. This in turn could enable the development of devices such as efficient spin-polarized tunnel diodes, spin-polarized barriers, and spin-polarized superconductors. This could also enable the development of p-type spin-polarized materials, such as p-type spin-polarized silicon, to improve power efficiency in transistors. This could involve the replacement of the expensive and difficult to produce Heusler compound GdPtSb with a more practical alternative, such as the less expensive and easier to produce material YbAgSb. This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.
