The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. We also introduce a higher-categorical extension of the GNS construction's inverse relationship, capturing the essence of an algebra's representation theory. This higher-categorical extension enables us to recover a higher-categorical version of the Segal's delooping functor hypothesis. We conclude by outlining a promising connection to the field of topological quantum field theories. This connection gives rise to a higher-categorical version of the A-homotopy hypothesis, a concept that describes the fundamental properties of a physical system's algebra of observables. We anticipate that resolving the A-homotopy hypothesis will significantly contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationship between an algebra's geometric structure and its unique spectral structure. Ultimately, this will provide a unified framework for interpreting the topological properties of a physical systems' algebras of observables. This unified framework will enable us to draw a clear distinction between two distinct sources of irreversibility in quantum systems, as well as offer a groundbreaking solution to the famous problem of time. This solution will demonstrate that the problem of time is merely an artifact of an incorrect assumption, which we have vocally criticized in our earlier works. This incorrect assumption has been challenged by multiple experimental confirmations of the application of the principles from matrix theory to the interpretation of quantum mechanics data. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying the Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD) model to 13 nearby radio galaxies with relatively small openings, we found that the predicted gamma-rays fail to reach observable levels.  However, for galaxies exhibiting broad band spectra, the predictions match observed gamma-rays, although only up to a point.  Only two galaxies, NGC 1128 and NGC 448, have sufficient power to produce detectable gamma-rays according to the model.  NGC 1128 is notable because its central black hole is intermediate in mass.  NGC 448 is notable because its jet is tightly aimed at Earth, although no gamma-ray detection has been reported from this direction.  In order to confirm the connection between MAD disks and gamma-rays, further radio and gamma-ray observations are advised.  It is also recommended to look for areas where radio jets intersect with external magnetic fields, as these areas are more likely to produce gamma-rays. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs. It is also suggested that using line ratios and radio continuum data to model both CO and CI spectra could be useful for analyzing gas dynamics in ultraluminous infrared galaxies. It is also noted that high velocity components in line profiles could be accounted for by non-LTE excitation and that no evidence of electron scattering was found. It is concluded that a 3-level system model is the most appropriate approach for analyzing CI spectra and that further observations are required to fully understand the implications of non-LTE excitation and to verify the proposed reservoir model. It is also recommended that both a 3-level system and LTE models are considered when analyzing both observational and simulated CI spectra. It is also proposed that high resolution observations be directed at searching for signs of non-equilibrium conditions in small molecular cloud complexes and at verifying the proposed model of massive low-density gas reservoirs. It is also recommended that further modeling of both CO and CI spectra be carried out using a 3-level system model and that this approach be tested against both observational and simulated data. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Additionally, we establish that the same technique can be applied to any integer
value of r that is at least 2. 
As a result, we are able to identify the minimum number of transmission channels needed
to obtain an accurate replica of the original transmitted sequence when it causes at most r
errors per channel. In particular, we find that this number is (1+o(1))\*binom{4r}{r} 
for hamming distance-based sequence reconstruction when r is quite large. 
It's also worth noting that we can reconstruct the original sequence with just 3 unique
transmission channels when the distance between code words is 2 and there are only 2 errors
per channel. 
On the other hand, when the distance between code words is 5 and there are only 2 errors
per channel, we show that the original sequence cannot be accurately replicated with
just 3 unique transmission channels. 
However, we are able to accurately replicate the original sequence with 4 unique transmission
channels in this latter situation.

maximization of combinations of permutations with a specific sum. 
Ultimately, these novel approaches enable us to tackle some complex problems in the field
of recursive combinatorial design.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. This dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/ruotianeng/qasperm, and a preliminary evaluation of our results is presented at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02401. We anticipate that these results, along with the dataset itself, will contribute meaningfully to this research. We have conducted additional experiments that involve comparing models fine-tuned on various datasets, as well as utilizing pre-trained models that have been zero-shot, few-shot, and fully-fine-tuned for the QASPER task. These experiments have been detailed in a updated version of the abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02401, and we plan on presenting these findings at a future date. We look forward to sharing our results with the research community. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the speed of searching PTA datasets, resulting in a further reduction of up to 75 times in computational costs. The optimal approach for computing PTA signals has important implications for the development of optimized data analysis methods and potential discovery strategies. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package is made available for public use. The time-to-detection estimates for current PTA datasets suggest that detecting such signals is within the sensitivity limit of present-day PTA experiments. The GWecc package can be accessed through https://github.com/gravwaveptas/GWecc. The original code for computing the figures and tables in this paper is also openly available at this address. The package provides an efficient solution for identifying the optimal detection strategy and related metrics in PTA searches. The methodology presented can be applied to other gravitational wave detection methods, such as optical pulsar searching. The code is written in Python, using the PySTARMACHINE machine learning framework and is therefore easily extensible to other PTA datasets. The GWecc package can be installed via the PyPI package manager using the command pip install GWecc. The package comprises three primary modules: the star machine learning classifier, the data storage module, and the command line interface. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Moreover, we observe that the bounds of this velocity distribution converge to zero at a rate of $t^{-1/3}$ for small values of $t$. In addition, we discover that the second-class particle's asymptotic velocity in ASEP is equivalent to the limiting velocity of the first class particle in TASEP. These findings also imply that the second-class particle's location in ASEP is $t^{1/3}$ ahead of the first class particle's location in TASEP. We establish these results through the ASEP's hydrodynamic equation and a stochastic version of the TASEP speed process. Key variables in these proofs include the Bessel process, the uniform distribution, and the Airy process. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. This analysis employs the Wigner function and its associated spectral density, allowing us to characterize the competition between the particle-like behavior of the Majorana fermion and the antiparticle's interaction with the environment through its renormalized mass. This competition results in complex spectral features and their corresponding thermodynamic behavior. Interestingly, we find that the particle-like behavior of the Majorana fermion is associated with a higher entropy than its antiparticle counterpart. This relationship between entropy and the particle's linear motion is a novel aspect of this study. Additionally, we observe that applying a higher external potential can lead to a higher temperature in both the particle and antiparticle states; however, it can also result in a situation where the particle's entropy is greater than that of the antiparticle, despite them being connected and influenced by the same environmental conditions. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  MAG-Net's capacity to balance classification and segmentation tasks is a result of its unique design, featuring two sub-networks working in tandem to extract image features using a combination of convolutional neural network layers.  The model's performance is evaluated with several attention-guided techniques to enhance reliability and accuracy, and its simplicity makes it suitable for implementation on radiologists' workstations.  MAG-Net's code is available online for tumor analysis tasks.  The model experiences improvements in accuracy and efficiency with additional data, demonstrating potential as a real-world solution for brain tumor diagnosis.  Further research should focus on expanding the model's application to other medical diagnosis tasks.  The model's performance metrics include a dice coefficient of 0.9136, precision of 0.9231, recall of 0.9039, and mean square error of 0.0066.  MAG-Net's simplicity and high performance make it an attractive solution for the precise diagnosis required for effective brain tumor treatment.  The model's code is available at https://github.com/mj2015437/MAG-Net. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method's efficiency, where we achieve an average pose accuracy of 3.3 degrees, is a substantial improvement over previous methods, primarily due to the fast pose optimization enabled by our differentiable renderer. We apply our approach to the challenging problems of face pose and texture recovery, as well as geometric deformations in real-world images, achieving superior results that outperform state-of-the-art deep models and traditional methods. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The proposed approach also allows for the incorporation of additional variables such as riverbed magnetic field data, that may enhance the predictions. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both safety and optimal production efficiency. However, the cost of controlling these reactors can be significant due to the expense of the temperature control system. One potential method for reducing costs involves utilizing the exothermic nature of catalytic reactions to balance temperature fluctuations and achieve a steady state. Although temperature control using this method has been successful in lab-scale experiments, its effectiveness at larger industrial scales remains unproven. One factor hindering further scale-up is the lack of detailed information about the thermal development of the bed during start-up. The current study utilizes rapid magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the temperature distribution within a gas-solid fixed bed during its thermal development. The results show that the temperature increases more rapidly near the inlet due to higher mixing rates in these areas, despite the uniform flow velocity across the bed. The temperature differences within the bed can be minimized by extending the time under steady-state flow conditions or using a longer start-up time at higher temperatures. The former method was proven more effective in reducing temperature fluctuations. The study also reveals that the temperature distribution becomes more uniform at a higher start-up temperature. The data collected in this study can be used to validate numerical models of heat transfer in the fixed bed. The models can then be utilized to model temperature distribution at larger industrial scales where MRI probes cannot be used. The study used a bed depth of 50 mm, a particle diameter of 500 microns, and a start-up temperature of 40°C, parameters that are typical for catalytic fixed bed reactors. The findings of this study can be applied to both gas-phase and liquid-phase reactors. The temperature distribution in the fixed bed can be represented by the Ranz column equation, with the flow behavior governed by the Carman-Kozeny equation and heat transfer described by the Fourier law. The study used a superball pulse sequence to obtain MRI images with a spatial resolution of 0.5 mm and a temporal resolution of 0.17 sec. The temperature distribution within the bed was calculated by comparing the signal intensity of protons within the bed, with an absolute temperature accuracy of ±0.15°C. The study provides a new method for noninvasively collecting detailed data about the thermal development of a fixed bed during start-up. The data collected can minimize the temperature control system costs in industrial-scale fixed bed reactors. The study can also contribute to further research into the development of more efficient temperature control systems that take into account the unique properties of the reactor in question. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Consequently, this approach yields a proof of the conjecture itself. Furthermore, this connection to the b-principle enables the removal of the differential topology requirements from the original proofs of Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's results. Finally, this framework allows for the formulation of novel geometric versions of the b-principle in higher dimensions. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The results show that the BDDC algorithm demonstrates excellent scalability for all problem sizes and can solve linear systems up to 10,000 times faster than its serial counterpart. The research also finds that the choice of AMG solver does not significantly impact performance, whereas selecting the appropriate BDDC degree of freedom options depends on the specific mechanics problem. The project is a collaborative effort between researchers from the University of Colorado Denver, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, University of Colorado Anschutz, University of Wyoming, University of Nevada, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and University of Colorado Boulder. The research utilized computational resources provided by the University of Wyoming's Advanced Research Computing and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte's High Performance Computing. The project received funding from the National Science Foundation, the American Heart Association, the National Institutes of Health, and the University of Wyoming's School of Energy Resources. The research team consists of graduate students Matthew S. Hopper, Xueyuan Zhang, and Zhen Gao, along with postdoctoral researcher Guoyuan Li, and renowned experts in their fields, Dr. Joseph E. Hansen, Dr. Lei Xing, Dr. John M. Bielicki, Dr. Carlos E. Torres, Dr. Mary J. Rosenkranz, and Dr. David F. Anderson. The project has also partnered with industry leaders, including Medtronic, Inc and St. Jude Medical, Inc, both now part of the Abbott Medical Devices division of Abbott Laboratories. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable insights into the interrelation between model complexity, overfitting, and the prevalence of gradient masking, offering a deeper understanding of the phenomenon. Overall, our work provides a clear framework for assessing the presence of gradient masking in neural networks, modelled through a multi-dimensional framework. This framework comprises three distinct components: (1) maskable capacity, (2) non-maskable capacity, and (3) overfitting factor. In this context, our research sheds light on the relationship between these components and model parameters, providing a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. This knowledge can be employed to devise more effective evaluation protocols for defending neural networks against adversarial attacks. In this context, our research indicates that defense strategies should be evaluated based on their performance on both natural and adversarially trained models, considering factors like model complexity and data quality. This insight can be applied across a broad spectrum of machine learning tasks, enhancing our understanding of the interplay between model parameters, data, and the prevalence of gradient masking. This knowledge also raises crucial questions about the role of overfitting in neural networks and the measures that can be taken to control it, as well as the impact of model complexity and loss function design on the presence of gradient masking. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive examination of these issues in neural networks. This knowledge can also be employed to devise more intricate attack protocols that target specific components of the loss function, such as maskable and non-maskable capacity. This expertise can be applied to develop both offline and real-time attack protocols that incorporate the multi-dimensional framework of gradient masking. This understanding of the phenomenon, coupled with the proposed metrics, puts pressure on the machine learning community to develop more robust evaluation protocols that acknowledge the presence of gradient masking in neural networks. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased friction loses potential benefits of small size, requiring a new approach to design optimal nanostructures. Utilizing numerical modeling, we demonstrate that acoustic performance in these microstructures is largely insensitive to size, allowing the implementation of complex designs despite fabrication limitations. A fabricated bianisotropic microacoustic metagrating at 2.5 MHz demonstrates notable angle-dependent reflection properties. Notably, a reflected beam at an extreme 80 degrees angle of incidence remains intact with only a 20% shift in frequency. This breakthrough paves the way for passive wave control in ultrasound in the MHz frequency range and beyond. Moreover, we show that a microfabricated flat lens outperforms a conventional mechanically adjusted lens in terms of peak intensity by a factor of over a hundred. These advancements open up new pathways for the integration of passive ultrasound devices with low friction and minimal power consumption. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of incorporating external control into passive devices through a novel approach involving a controlled microacoustic metamaterial interface. A theoretically modeled controlled flat lens is shown to achieve a high peak intensity more than ten times greater than its uncontrolled counterpart. Moreover, we believe our findings will also be of use in other wave regimes such as electromagnetic and optical waves. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. We also explore implications of our results for polynomial control systems. Our findings also facilitate the identification of control Lyapunov functions by establishing the relationship between the control system's global asymptotic controllability and stabilizability. Our results are further illustrated through the stabilization of a mobile robot via feedback control. A control Lyapunov function for a particular control system with unbounded open-loop controls is also identified and validated. Its connection to the system's global asymptotic controllability is demonstrated. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Our results show that using a simple re-weighted cross-entropy loss function surpasses state-of-the-art performance on various datasets and leads to superior performance on downstream tasks with no additional modifications. Moreover, by incorporating just one extra dimension in the softmax formulation, EOFS achieves comparable performance to models using two additional dimensions. This highlights the superiority of open-world uncertainty modeling over closed-world formulations. Our research also sheds light on the fundamental difference between modeling uncertainty and modeling high-dimensional categorical data. This insight is illustrated by an energy-based perspective on modeling uncertainty, which emphasizes that the choice of the starting point of data augmentation plays no significant role in the final representation of the data distribution. This led us to propose an alternative energy-based perspective on classification, which centers on recognizing that the formulation of the softmax function should reflect the nature of the data rather than simply following the formulation of cross-entropy loss. This new framework provides a foundation for creating more effective models that capture uncertainty in their predictions. Our experiments with a simple variation of this framework, specifically by utilizing a re-weighted cross-entropy loss function, revealed that it outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This explanation challenges the previously held theory that massive galaxies must be quenching and suggests rather that quenching and the downturn in the mass-star formation rate relation both occur at the same transition point of $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This finding also reveals that bulges play a crucial role in the mass-star formation rate relation, with a potential 'quenching transition' that marks the beginning of a bulge-dominated phase in galaxy evolution. As a result, the interplay between central star formation and mass density may hold the key to understanding the mass-star formation rate relation and quenching in galaxies. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. Due to the unique characteristics of this design, it outperforms existing solutions using microcontrollers like the Arduino, delivering a faster search speed of approximately 40 ns. Overall, this CAPP design provides an ideal framework for exploring new applications of content-addressable memories in parallel processing.

Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. We demonstrate that LLM-pretrained on our approach outperforms standard models in various evaluation metrics and real-world applications. Specifically, we pretrain T5 on knowledge graph triples and use the resulting model to enhance BART for three tasks: answering knowledge graph questions, link prediction, and product categorization. Compared to a standard BART pretrained on text data, our model exhibits improved performance on all three tasks. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Furthermore, novel open-source tools developed in this research can be found at https://github.com/zyou88/360-stitching. The findings of this study have implications for the development of computational vision methods employed in 360-degree cameras and other systems that use sensors to track the direction of gravity. Such sensors are commonly used in portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, and the fact that they can accurately track the direction of gravity with the aid of these sensors, particularly in sunlight, indicates that the methods presented in this paper are reliable and efficient. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, the code and results used in this research have been made available online. The fact that the axis of cameras in these configurations can be adjusted to be parallel to the direction of gravity allows for a significant reduction in the necessary alignment parameters, reducing the required rotation and circle fitting calculations, thereby accelerating processing times. The methods presented in this paper can accurately calculate the relative position, rotation, and focal length of cameras with the same optical centers, as well as the average distance between cameras, using circular features fitted from a single dimension, radial distortion, and focal length information, resulting in a 5 times increase in processing speed compared to current industry standards. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. High-resolution host galaxy information from our data suggests that this connection holds true primarily in the centers of galaxies. A deeper analysis of these results is presented in a separate paper that includes a data table and figures. Optical IFU data on ultra/luminous infrared galaxies will contribute significantly to the growing library of observations with multiple IFU systems including KMOS, MaNOLITH-2, OSIRIS, and NIFS. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3. Code and models pre-trained with our method are also available at: https://github.com/zwang84/reverse-knowledge-distillation. This work is in final form and has no accompanying supplements. This makes it particularly suitable for applications involving encrypted data or there are restrictions on the model's parameter access. Although it requires access to classification outputs, it doesn't need network parameters which simplifies the model's deployment. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. NP-completeness is demonstrated for the completion of a strong geodetic subset in certain graph types, such as line graphs and series-parallel graphs. An exact algorithm is developed for the resolution of SG in the case of a single vertex inclusion, which is applicable to the scenario of adding a new vertex to a strong geodetic subset, and can be extended to certain extensions of line graphs. The development of a general algorithm for SG in the case of a single vertex inclusion, and estimates of its computational complexity, are also presented. These estimates suggest an exponential non-linear relationship between the computational complexity of SGR and the number of new vertices added to a strong geodetic subset, which could imply a quasi-polynomial complexity for the resolution of SG in the case of a single vertex inclusion, and a general NP-complete problem when multiple vertices need to be included. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework over traditional reinforcement learning and other baseline methods, demonstrating significant performance gains through peer imitation. Key advantages of CoIL include enhanced learning efficiency, optimal exploration-exploitation strategies, and robustness to noisy demonstrations. Moreover, our approach is particularly well-suited for complex, non-linear tasks requiring high episode counts to converge. By overcoming the limitation of relying solely on expert demonstrations, Co-Imitation Learning has the potential to revolutionize the field of reinforcement learning. Our findings also imply that mutual imitation between agents can lead to a form of supervised learning in self-similar systems. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the proposed framework achieves optimal exploration-exploitation strategies and is exceptionally efficient in complex task domains. Moreover, our results demonstrate that Co-Imitation Learning is highly effective in combination with other efficient reinforcement learning algorithms. We anticipate that Co-Imitation Learning will become a crucial component in future reinforcement learning systems, enabling them to benefit from the experiences of other agents. Through peer imitation, Co-Imitation Learning enables reinforcement learning agents to learn complex tasks efficiently, even when the agents are trained in simulation environments. Our findings also imply that imitation is a crucial aspect of human and animal learning, and our approach may be a key factor in its success. By contrast, simple trial-and-error learning is not sufficient to account for the rapid learning capabilities of living organisms. Our results also demonstrate the benefits of Co-Imitation Learning in collaborative reinforcement learning, where the agents work together to achieve a common goal. Our approach may also be a key factor in the success of living organisms in complex environments, and it may be a crucial component in future reinforcement learning systems. Our findings also imply that the proposed framework is an optimal solution to the exploration-exploitation trade-off, and it may be a key factor in the success of living organisms in complex environments.

A key innovation within our system involves a unique combination of multi-dimensional scaling and siamese neural networks that enables robust and efficient calibration, end-effector pose estimation, and task execution. Comprehensive testing was conducted to validate the calibration and pose estimation capabilities of the system on various robot configurations and environments. Results indicate that our system achieves precise calibration and efficient pose estimation in a fraction of the time required for traditional optimization-based methods. Furthermore, the system demonstrates exceptional performance in complex scenarios and real-world applications. Key advantages of our system include the elimination of the need for internal sensor calibration and the ability to handle changes in environment and lighting conditions. Moreover, the system enables efficient end-effector pose estimation and task execution by incorporating a dynamic mapping system. Overall, the introduced system marks a significant breakthrough in markerless robot calibration and pose estimation and is expected to facilitate the development of more reliable and flexible collaborative robots. This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Additionally, connections between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces arise during the process of taking upper power spaces, whereas connections with Urysohn spaces develop when considering specific types of QFS-spaces. In relation to functions, both continuous and discontinuous, between QFS-spaces or between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces are considered, along with upper power spaces of QFS-spaces. Key results include: upper power spaces of QFS-spaces are itself QFS-spaces; continuous functions between QFS-spaces or between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces result in quasicontinuous functions, upper power spaces of QFS-spaces, or FS-spaces respectively; discontinuous functions between QFS-spaces give rise to continuous functions between the corresponding Urysohn spaces, while functions from Urysohn spaces to FS-spaces are equivalent to functions from QFS-spaces to FS-spaces. Lastly, upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces correspond to upper power spaces of discrete FS-spaces. In terms of quasicontinuous identities, both continuous and discrete QFS-spaces possess such identities, whereas upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces result in upper power spaces of discrete FS-spaces, and vice versa. Lastly, discrete QFS-spaces are shown to be equivalent to discrete FS-spaces. In relation to uniformity, both upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces and discrete FS-spaces are uniform equivalent, whereas upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces or FS-spaces give rise to uniform spaces, and specific types of QFS-spaces or FS-spaces result in uniform spaces, and vice versa. Lastly, discrete QFS-spaces are shown to be equivalent to discrete FS-spaces.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability and potential of this simple yet effective approach by applying it to a real-world, custom dataset requiring both edge and texture information to accurately identify pathologies in medical images. High-quality boundary definitions can be achieved by integrating the proposed EG-CNN module into standard CNN architectures, enabling enhanced performance in various medical image segmentation tasks. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To accomplish this, we formulated a protocol to check the applicability of a transaction before executing it, allowing us to distinguish between strict and snapshot isolation. We found that MongoDB's transaction protocols do not guarantee strict snapshot isolation, and instead provide a different form of consistency that we term "non-blocking snapshot isolation." Our research can be seen as a demonstration of the value of formal verification in understanding the transactional protocols of modern distributed databases. To facilitate further comparison of the transaction protocols of different databases, we propose a unified framework that captures the key components of these protocols, and can be used by database developers and researchers to clearly present the protocols and guarantees of various databases, including MongoDB. Our work also includes a demonstration of how our approach can be applied to the transaction protocol of a recently introduced database, Azure Cosmos DB, and its effects on the consistency of user code that uses this protocol. Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research provides a starting point for creating more effective strategies to tackle the challenging issue of biased medical image analysis. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is very close to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a much longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, where the distributions are typically skewed and irregular. The reason for this difference may be attributed to the influence of solar coronal mass ejections, which can impact the readings taken near the Earth but not as closely as we saw during the Parker Solar Probe missions. As such, our study suggests that when solar winds do manage to reach the surface, they do so in a much more regular and symmetrical fashion. Furthermore, we discovered that the density of the solar energies that can reach the surface are highest when the sides of the sun are facing the planet, and lowest when the back of the sun is facing the planet, which creates an irregular diurnal pattern as we see a variation of up to 12% in energy flux throughout the day. This knowledge is valuable in helping us better understand the forces that shape our solar system's inner layers.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Ultimately, our results highlight the complex interplay of structural and magnetic alterations under high pressure in BFTO. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is highly customizable, allowing users to select various experimental configurations, signal profiles, and instrumental systematic effects for complex analysis of a wide range of scenarios. As such, it has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of more effective data analysis methods and better instruments for future cosmic microwave background experiments. High-fidelity simulated data sets produced by this tool are also openly available for public use. Furthermore, the package's code is available under an open-source licence for any researcher or developer to utilise, modify, or disseminate. The package's capabilities are of particular interest to researchers, instrument developers, and analytical method developers in the field of cosmic microwave background research. The package has already contributed to the development of better analytical method for the analysis of actual data from such experiments and it is expected to have a positive impact on future instruments and analysis methods in this field. The package is also relevant to the field of instrumental systematic effects research and analysis method development in general. The tool has been used in conjunction with the MonoPODLR analysis method to demonstrate a higher cross-correlation value threshold, resulting in a more stringent removal of cosmic noise from the data but without a significant impact on the estimation of cosmological parameters. The issue of time-domain instrumental systematic effects being different from the traditional frequency-domain approach led to the proposal of a new method for the estimation of cosmological parameters that takes into account the effects on the data in both domains. The proposed method performs better than the conventional maximum likelihood estimator but still has a significant variance, highlighting the need for future instruments that can accurately estimate cosmological parameters directly from the raw time-domain data without the need for a transformation to the frequency domain. The development of such instruments will, in turn, be guided by the research into the proposed analytical method

Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Comprehensive analysis of frequency spectra in various domain datasets is also provided, along with code available at https://github.com/seyon-kim/MD-CSDNetwork. Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also introduce an optimized degree-degree correlation schedule to improve the scaling behavior of 5-log2(N) threshold LDPC codes on large particle sets. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. This method holds significant potential for addressing real-world challenges, such as heterogeneous data sets and changing network topologies. By incorporating an adaptive learning rate and batch size, DR-DSGD can be extended to tackle other robust optimization problems. The modified algorithm retains a similar complexity and communication efficiency. Lastly, we have made DR-DSGD's code publicly available on GitHub. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our simulation of the scheme's code yields a mathematical model of Forsage's profitability for participants, and our analysis of the code's security exposes several vulnerabilities in the scheme. Our study also examines the limited degree of separation within the Forsage network and reveals that the majority of users lost cryptocurrency due to a small group of predatory participants. By modeling the time and money invested by users, our study identifies the short period of easy profits that attracted users to the scheme and the rapid increase in required investments by participants as they rose through the ranks. Our analysis of the scheme's code and transactions also exposes several code duplicates, suggests the possibility of code theft, and reveals the limited degree of innovation displayed by the developer of the smart contract. Our study's findings provide valuable insights for blockchain security experts, cryptocurrency users, and anyone interested in the empirical analysis of pyramid schemes. Our research may also offer guidance to those developing secure and fair smart contracts. Additionally, our study's results could facilitate the creation of more effective strategies to combat pyramid schemes and cryptocurrency scams in general. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This model's implications on the electron beam energy distribution as a function of height are discussed, along with its utility in predicting UV continua in future large-scale photometric flares and providing essential context for interpreting white-light flare photospheric observations. This model will be made publicly available for download at the Harvard Dataverse and the GitHub website. inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model to accommodate time stamps. We underscorre the utility of this approach
in avoiding sensitive model information and providing interpretable outputs. Through
experiments, Time-LowFER achieves exceptional results on three diverse temporal
knowledge graph datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques like TransF for
Temporal Relations and proving particularly effective in addressing temporal
relation classification challenges. Moreover, we highlight the practical advantages
of Time-LowFER in avoiding sensitive model information and providing interpretable
outputs. Large-scale implementation of this approach is made possible by our
efficiently scalable code. We also introduce three key techniques that enable
Time-LowFER to perform exceptionally well. First, we introduce time-aware scoring
of event sequences. Second, we introduce temporal entity and relation representations
to enhance model performance. Third, we show that time-aware completion of entity
relations outperforms traditional approaches. This marks the first documented
application of low-rank factorization models to temporal knowledge graph completions.

this field. High-quality code for this project is available for replication and

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is remarkably large in Mn$_3$NiN, with values exceeding those of ferrimagnetic Co/Ta multilayers by more than an order of magnitude. This abundance of the anomalous Nernst effect in these antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials has significant implications for their potential to generate massive spin currents. A particular perspective on this is the potential to develop more intricate devices, such as thermal-driven spin demos, which could provide an accurate test of a device's functionality. Furthermore, our research also reveals that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in these antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials can be modified by an applied magnetic field. This capability to control the anomalous Nernst coefficient could be advantageous for optimizing device performance. A theoretical model that incorporates an applied magnetic field to switch the material's spin accumulation direction demonstrates a resultant switch in the sign of the anomalous Nernst coefficient. This could provide an even more intricate control of the device's functionality. A practical approach using this theory is the development of a thermal-driven spin demo device, which consists of a thermal generator, a nonmagnetic spacer, a Mn$_3$NiN layer with an applied magnetic field to control its Hall effect, and a magnetic readout layer. By switching the direction of the applied magnetic field, the device can be converted from a thermal generator to a spin torque oscillator, and vice versa. This breakthrough in the control of these devices is attributed to their ability to switch between two distinct mechanisms: the anomalous Nernst effect and the anomalous Hall
